# Vocabulary

> Part of **InferenceLearn**, a free course on LLM inference engineering. Web version: vocabulary.html. Whole course in one file: llms-full.txt

// item descriptions

Every term in the course in plain English. Most come with a "≈" analogy to make them stick. Search the list, or switch to **flashcards** to drill them.

## Basics

- **Inference**: Running a trained model on new inputs to produce outputs. No learning happens, only forward passes. Training is writing the cookbook; inference is cooking from it for every customer.
- **Token**: The unit an LLM reads and writes: an integer ID from the tokenizer's vocabulary. An English token is about ¾ of a word. Lego bricks that text is built from.
- **Tokenizer**: Converts text to token IDs and back (e.g. BPE). Its vocabulary usually has 32k–256k entries.
- **Embedding**: A learned vector (e.g. 4096 numbers) looked up for each token ID. It's the model's internal representation of the token.
- **Logits**: The model's raw, unnormalized scores, one for every vocabulary token. Softmax turns them into probabilities.
- **Softmax**: Turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1: exp(xᵢ) ÷ Σ exp(xⱼ).
- **Autoregressive decoding**: Generating one token at a time and feeding each new token back in as input for the next step. Writing a sentence where you can only see the words you've already written.
- **Prefill**: The first phase of a request: process the whole prompt in parallel, build its KV cache, and produce the first token. Compute-bound. Reading the whole question before you start answering.
- **Decode**: The phase that produces output tokens one per step. Each step reads all the weights for very little math, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound.
- **Greedy decoding**: Always picking the single most likely next token (argmax). Deterministic, but can be repetitive.
- **Temperature**: Divides logits before softmax. Below 1 makes outputs more focused, above 1 more random, and 0 means greedy. A creativity dial.
- **Top-k sampling**: Sample only from the k most likely tokens.
- **Top-p (nucleus) sampling**: Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p (e.g. 0.95). The set grows when the model is unsure.
- **EOS token**: End-of-sequence token. When the model emits it, generation for that request stops.
- **Context length**: The number of tokens (prompt plus output) a sequence holds. The KV cache grows linearly with it.
- **Self-attention**: The layer where each token computes a query, key and value, and mixes in information from earlier tokens weighted by query·key similarity.
- **Causal mask**: Stops a token from attending to future tokens. It's why past keys and values never change, and so why they can be cached.

## GPU & hardware

- **GPU**: A massively parallel processor with thousands of cores and specialized matrix units. The workhorse of LLM inference.
- **Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)**: One of the GPU's many independent compute units (132 on an H100 SXM). Each has cores, tensor cores, registers and shared memory. One kitchen station in a huge restaurant.
- **Tensor cores**: Specialized units for very fast matrix multiply-accumulate at low precision (BF16, FP8, FP4). Most of a GPU's FLOPs come from them.
- **HBM**: High-Bandwidth Memory: the GPU's main memory (e.g. 80 GB at ~3.35 TB/s on H100). It holds the weights and KV cache. The warehouse: huge, but a walk away.
- **SRAM / shared memory**: Small, very fast on-chip memory per SM (~228 KB on H100). Kernels stage tiles of data here. The cutting board: tiny, but right under your hands.
- **Memory bandwidth**: How many bytes per second can move between HBM and the compute units. It sets decode speed.
- **FLOPs**: Floating-point operations. A forward pass costs about 2 × parameters FLOPs per token. FLOP/s (per second) measures compute speed.
- **Arithmetic intensity**: FLOPs done per byte moved from memory. For LLM linear layers in BF16 it's roughly the number of tokens in the batch. How much cooking you do per trip to the warehouse.
- **Roofline model**: Attainable performance = min(peak FLOP/s, intensity × bandwidth). It tells you which limit you'll hit first.
- **Ridge point**: Peak FLOP/s ÷ bandwidth: the intensity where a GPU switches from memory-bound to compute-bound (~295 FLOP/byte on H100).
- **Memory-bound**: Limited by how fast data moves, not by math. Compute units sit idle waiting for bytes. Typical of decode.
- **Compute-bound**: Limited by math throughput. Memory keeps up and the tensor cores are the bottleneck. Typical of prefill and large batches.
- **BF16**: bfloat16: a 16-bit float with FP32's range (8-bit exponent) but less precision. The default serving precision.
- **NVLink**: NVIDIA's high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU link (~900 GB/s per GPU on H100). Essential for fast tensor parallelism.
- **PCIe**: The general-purpose bus between GPU and CPU (~64 GB/s each way for PCIe 5 x16). Much slower than NVLink.

## Metrics

- **TTFT**: Time To First Token: from sending the request to receiving the first token. Includes queueing and prefill. How long until the waiter says "coming right up".
- **ITL**: Inter-Token Latency: the gap between consecutive streamed tokens.
- **TPOT**: Time Per Output Token: a request's average decode time per token, (E2E − TTFT) ÷ (tokens − 1).
- **E2E latency**: End-to-end time for the full response ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1).
- **Throughput**: Work done per second across all users, usually output tokens/s. Higher throughput means lower cost per token.
- **Goodput**: Throughput counting only requests that met their latency SLOs. Pizzas delivered hot, not just pizzas delivered.
- **SLO**: Service Level Objective: a latency or availability target, e.g. "p90 TTFT under 500 ms".
- **Percentile latency (p50/p99)**: p99 = 99% of requests are faster than this. Tail percentiles reveal spikes that averages hide.
- **Little's law**: Concurrency = throughput × latency. 20 req/s × 10 s means ~200 requests in flight.
- **MFU**: Model FLOPs Utilization: achieved FLOP/s ÷ peak. The efficiency metric for compute-bound work.
- **MBU**: Model Bandwidth Utilization: achieved bytes/s ÷ peak bandwidth. The efficiency metric for decode. 60–80% is good.
- **Cost per million tokens**: GPU $/hour ÷ (tokens/s × 3600) × 10⁶. The number that ends up on the invoice.

## Memory & KV cache

- **KV cache**: Stored key and value vectors for all previous tokens, so each decode step only computes the new token's K/V. Size = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes, per token. Notes from earlier in the conversation, so you don't reread the whole chat every time.
- **KV head**: A key/value head. With GQA, several query heads share one, so fewer KV heads means a smaller cache.
- **KV cache quantization**: Storing K/V in FP8, INT8 or INT4 to halve or quarter cache memory and bandwidth.
- **Fragmentation**: Wasted memory: reserved-but-unused space (internal) or free gaps too small to use (external). PagedAttention mostly eliminates it.
- **Prefix caching**: Reusing KV for prompt prefixes shared across requests (system prompts, chat history), so prefill skips them.
- **RadixAttention**: SGLang's prefix cache, organized as a radix tree over token sequences, with token-level matching and natural branching.
- **Reference counting**: Tracking how many running sequences use a KV block. Only blocks with count 0 may be evicted.
- **LRU eviction**: Least-Recently-Used: when memory is needed, drop the cached block that was used longest ago.
- **Copy-on-write**: Sequences share the same physical KV blocks until one of them writes something different. Only then is a private copy made.
- **KV offloading**: Moving cold KV blocks from GPU memory to CPU RAM, SSD or remote storage, and loading them back when needed.
- **Cache hit rate**: The fraction of prompt tokens served from the prefix cache. A sudden drop often means a prompt template changed.

## Batching & scheduling

- **Batch size**: How many sequences are processed together in one forward step. Bigger batches amortize weight reads.
- **Static batching**: Form a batch, pad it, and run until every sequence finishes. Simple but wasteful. A bus that won't leave until the last passenger arrives, and won't let anyone on mid-route.
- **Dynamic batching**: Wait a short window or until the batch is full, then run. Good for fixed-cost models, but still request-level.
- **Continuous batching**: Iteration-level scheduling: sequences join and leave the running batch at every decode step. Also called in-flight batching. A conveyor-belt sushi bar: seats free up and fill instantly.
- **Ragged batch**: A batch whose sequences have different lengths, packed without padding. Kernels get per-sequence offsets.
- **Head-of-line blocking**: New work stuck waiting behind slow work already in progress.
- **Chunked prefill**: Splitting a long prompt's prefill into chunks that share engine steps with running decodes, so token streams don't freeze.
- **Token budget**: The maximum number of tokens (prefill chunks plus decodes) processed in one engine step, e.g. vLLM's max-num-batched-tokens.
- **Preemption**: Evicting a running sequence when KV memory runs out, then recomputing or swapping its cache in later.
- **Admission control**: Deciding whether to accept, queue or reject new requests, so the system doesn't overload and collapse.

## Attention

- **MHA**: Multi-Head Attention: every query head has its own key and value head. Best quality, biggest KV cache.
- **MQA**: Multi-Query Attention: all query heads share a single K/V head. The smallest cache, with some quality risk.
- **GQA**: Grouped-Query Attention: groups of query heads share a K/V head (e.g. 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads), so the cache is 4× smaller than MHA. Roommates sharing one fridge instead of each buying their own.
- **MLA**: Multi-head Latent Attention (DeepSeek): caches a compressed low-rank latent instead of full per-head K/V.
- **FlashAttention**: An IO-aware exact attention kernel. It tiles Q/K/V in on-chip SRAM and never writes the N×N score matrix to HBM.
- **Online softmax**: Computing softmax chunk by chunk with a running max and sum, rescaling earlier results as you go. This makes tiling possible.
- **PagedAttention**: Stores the KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous blocks, like OS virtual-memory pages, to remove fragmentation. A library storing a book's chapters on any free shelf, with an index card saying where each one is.
- **Block table**: The per-sequence map from logical KV blocks to physical memory blocks in PagedAttention.
- **Flash-Decoding**: Splits the KV sequence across thread blocks during decode, so even small batches with long contexts use the whole GPU.
- **Sliding-window attention**: Each token attends only to the last W tokens, which caps KV size per layer.

## Quantization

- **Quantization**: Storing numbers in fewer bits (8, 4…) to cut memory and bandwidth. Done well, with little quality loss. Saving a photo as a smaller JPEG.
- **Scale & zero point**: The mapping between real and integer values: q = round(x/s) + z, x̂ = s·(q − z). Symmetric quantization uses z = 0.
- **Per-group quantization**: One scale per small group of weights (e.g. 128), so an outlier only hurts its own group.
- **W4A16 / W8A8**: Notation for weight bits / activation bits. W4A16 = INT4 weights with BF16 math (weight-only). W8A8 = 8-bit weights and activations.
- **FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2)**: 8-bit floating-point formats with native tensor-core support on Hopper and newer. A common near-lossless choice.
- **FP4 (NVFP4 / MXFP4)**: 4-bit float formats with small-block scales, natively supported by Blackwell tensor cores.
- **Outliers**: A few activation channels with values 10–100× larger than the rest. They wreck naive INT8 scaling. One giant in a class photo forces everyone else to be tiny.
- **SmoothQuant**: Moves activation outliers into the weights with an equivalent per-channel rescaling, enabling W8A8.
- **GPTQ**: Post-training quantization that uses second-order (Hessian) information to compensate for each rounding error column by column.
- **AWQ**: Activation-aware Weight Quantization: scales up salient weight channels (those multiplied by large activations) before quantizing.
- **Calibration set**: A few hundred sample inputs used to measure activation ranges and statistics during post-training quantization.
- **PTQ**: Post-Training Quantization: quantizing an already-trained model without retraining it.
- **GGUF**: llama.cpp's single-file model format, with many quantization types (e.g. Q4_K_M).

## Decoding tricks

- **Speculative decoding**: Draft several tokens cheaply, then verify them all in one target-model pass. The output distribution is unchanged. An intern drafts the email; the boss approves several sentences at a glance.
- **Draft model**: The cheap proposer in speculative decoding: a small model, n-gram lookup, or extra heads.
- **Target model**: The big model whose output distribution you want. It verifies the drafts.
- **Acceptance rate**: α: the probability that a drafted token is accepted. Expected tokens per pass = (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α).
- **Rejection sampling**: Accept a draft token with probability min(1, p/q), otherwise resample from max(0, p − q). This makes speculation lossless.
- **EAGLE / Medusa**: Speculative methods that draft with lightweight heads attached to the target model instead of a separate model.
- **MTP**: Multi-Token Prediction: modules trained to predict several future tokens. They can serve as speculative drafts.
- **Tree attention**: Verifying a tree of alternative drafts in one pass with a special attention mask.
- **Structured output**: Constraining generation to a JSON schema or grammar by masking invalid tokens at each step.

## Parallelism

- **Tensor parallelism (TP)**: Splits each layer's weight matrices across GPUs, with all-reduces per layer. Lowers per-token latency. Four chefs each chopping a quarter of every vegetable.
- **Pipeline parallelism (PP)**: Splits a model by layers across GPUs. Works across nodes, but doesn't make a single token faster. An assembly line.
- **Pipeline bubble**: Idle time in pipeline stages while waiting for work. It's reduced by keeping several micro-batches in flight.
- **Data parallelism (DP)**: Independent model replicas with requests load-balanced across them. Scales throughput.
- **Expert parallelism (EP)**: Places different MoE experts on different GPUs and routes tokens to them with all-to-all communication.
- **MoE**: Mixture of Experts: a router sends each token to a few of many expert MLPs. Total parameters ≫ active parameters. A hospital: every patient sees only 2 specialists, but you employ 64.
- **Router (gating)**: The small network in an MoE layer that picks the top-k experts for each token.
- **All-reduce**: A collective operation that sums tensors across GPUs and gives everyone the result. TP needs two per transformer layer.
- **All-to-all**: A collective where every GPU sends a different chunk to every other GPU. Used for MoE token dispatch.
- **Context parallelism (CP)**: Splits one long sequence across GPUs (e.g. Ring Attention) for very long contexts.

## Kernels & compilers

- **Kernel**: A function launched on the GPU across a grid of thread blocks. Eager PyTorch runs roughly one kernel per op.
- **Kernel fusion**: Combining several ops into one kernel, so data stays in registers instead of round-tripping through HBM. Doing all the errands in one trip instead of three.
- **Kernel launch overhead**: A few µs of CPU time per kernel launch. Significant when a decode step launches hundreds of small kernels.
- **CUDA graph**: A recorded sequence of kernel launches that is replayed with a single launch. Removes CPU overhead in decode. A macro instead of typing every command.
- **Triton (language)**: A Python-embedded language and compiler for block-level GPU kernels. Not the same thing as Triton Inference Server.
- **torch.compile**: PyTorch's compiler. It captures the model graph and generates fused kernels (via TorchInductor/Triton).
- **CUTLASS**: NVIDIA's C++ template library (with CuTe) for building high-performance GEMM and attention kernels.
- **Nsight Systems**: NVIDIA's whole-system timeline profiler (`nsys`). Shows CPU threads, CUDA calls, kernels and the gaps between them.
- **Nsight Compute**: NVIDIA's per-kernel profiler (`ncu`): achieved bandwidth, occupancy, roofline position.

## Production systems

- **Inference engine**: Software that serves models efficiently: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and others.
- **Disaggregated serving**: Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and moving the KV cache between them. Separate prep kitchen and plating line.
- **KV-aware routing**: Sending a request to the replica that already caches its longest prefix, balanced against current load.
- **Session affinity**: Routing a conversation's requests to the same replica (e.g. by hashing the session ID) to keep cache hits.
- **Autoscaling**: Adding or removing replicas based on load signals such as queue depth, KV usage and latency against SLO.
- **Cold start**: The time for a new replica to become ready: pull the image, load the weights, compile, capture graphs. Often minutes.
- **OpenAI-compatible API**: The de-facto HTTP interface (/v1/chat/completions) that most engines expose, so any OpenAI client works.
- **SSE streaming**: Server-Sent Events: the server pushes each token to the client as soon as it's generated.
- **Capacity planning**: Estimating how many GPUs you need from traffic, token lengths, SLOs and benchmarked per-GPU capacity.
- **Load test (open-loop)**: Sending requests at a target arrival rate whether or not earlier ones have finished, like real traffic. It exposes queueing collapse.
- **Backpressure**: Signalling clients to slow down (HTTP 429/503) instead of queueing work forever.
- **Graceful drain**: On deploy or shutdown: stop admitting new requests, let in-flight streams finish, then restart.
- **Multi-LoRA serving**: Serving many small LoRA fine-tune adapters on one shared base model at the same time.

# Practice

> Part of **InferenceLearn**, a free course on LLM inference engineering. Web version: practice.html. Whole course in one file: llms-full.txt

// training grounds

Reading isn't learning until you can use it. Test yourself in the arcade, prepare for interviews, then work through the napkin-math workbook.

[[play] 45Quiz ArcadeMultiple-choice game with lives, streaks and a hi-score. Every answer comes with an explanation.](#arcade) [[prepare] 39Interview PrepReal-style interview questions with model answers, what the interviewer is testing, and follow-ups.](interview.md) [[think] 14WorkbookNapkin-math problems with hints and step-by-step solutions, explain-it-back prompts and experiments.](workbook.md)

*(An interactive quiz game runs here on the web page. The full question bank with answers is below.)*

## Question bank (study mode)

Every arcade question with its answer and explanation. Good for revision, or for an AI tutor to quiz you from.

**Show all 45 questions with answers**

1. Why is LLM decode usually memory-bandwidth-bound?
   A. Softmax is expensive
   B. Each step reads all the weights but does very little math per byte
   C. The tokenizer runs on the GPU
   D. Tensor cores can't do matrix-vector products
   **Answer: B.** One decode step multiplies the weights by a single token vector per sequence. That's about 2 FLOPs per weight read, far below the ~300 FLOP/byte an H100 needs to be compute-bound.
2. Which metric is mostly determined by the prefill phase?
   A. Inter-token latency
   B. TPOT
   C. Time to first token
   D. Output tokens/s per user
   **Answer: C.** Prefill processes the prompt and produces the first token, so it dominates TTFT (along with queueing).
3. What happens to the sampling distribution as temperature approaches 0?
   A. It becomes greedy (argmax)
   B. It becomes uniform
   C. It's unaffected
   D. The model refuses to answer
   **Answer: A.** Dividing logits by a tiny T exaggerates the gaps, so nearly all probability goes to the top token.
4. For a BF16 linear layer with batch B ≪ hidden size, arithmetic intensity is roughly…
   A. 1, always
   B. hidden_size
   C. B²
   D. B FLOPs per byte
   **Answer: D.** FLOPs = 2·B·d², bytes ≈ 2·d² (the weights), so AI ≈ B. More tokens per weight read means more math per byte.
5. Best-case single-user decode speed of an 8B BF16 model on an H100 (3.35 TB/s)?
   A. ~20 tok/s
   B. ~200 tok/s
   C. ~2,000 tok/s
   D. ~20,000 tok/s
   **Answer: B.** 16 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 4.8 ms per step, so ~209 tok/s at most. Real engines get a good fraction of that.
6. The ridge point of a GPU is…
   A. Its maximum clock speed
   B. The largest batch that fits in memory
   C. Peak FLOP/s divided by memory bandwidth
   D. The temperature at which it throttles
   **Answer: C.** Below that arithmetic intensity you're memory-bound; above it, compute-bound. It's ~295 FLOP/byte on an H100.
7. A service handles 30 req/s with 5 s average latency. By Little's law, how many requests are in flight?
   A. 150
   B. 6
   C. 35
   D. 0.17
   **Answer: A.** Concurrency = throughput × latency = 30 × 5 = 150.
8. What is "goodput"?
   A. Throughput including input tokens
   B. Peak tokens/s at maximum batch
   C. GPU utilization from nvidia-smi
   D. Throughput counting only requests that met their SLOs
   **Answer: D.** Goodput measures useful work: requests delivered within latency targets.
9. An H100 costs $3/hour and serves 3,000 output tok/s. Cost per 1M output tokens?
   A. ~$3.00
   B. ~$0.28
   C. ~$0.03
   D. ~$10.80
   **Answer: B.** 3,000 × 3,600 = 10.8M tokens/hour, and $3 ÷ 10.8 ≈ $0.28 per million.
10. Why are queries not stored in the KV cache?
   A. They're too large
   B. They're recomputed by the sampler
   C. Only the current token's query is ever needed
   D. Queries are stored in the embedding table
   **Answer: C.** Each step's new query attends over all cached keys and values. Past queries are never used again.
11. Llama-3-8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, BF16. KV cache per token?
   A. 128 KiB
   B. 16 KiB
   C. 512 KiB
   D. 1 MiB
   **Answer: A.** 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 B = 128 KiB.
12. Batching many sequences amortizes weight reads. Why doesn't it amortize KV-cache reads?
   A. The KV cache lives on the CPU
   B. KV reads are cached in L2
   C. Attention is compute-bound
   D. Each sequence has its own unique KV cache
   **Answer: D.** Weights are shared by every sequence, but every sequence's K/V is different and must be read separately.
13. Which change shrinks the KV cache without retraining the model?
   A. Switching MHA to GQA
   B. Storing the KV cache in FP8
   C. Adding more layers
   D. Using MLA
   **Answer: B.** KV-cache quantization is a serving-time choice. GQA and MLA are architectural and decided at training time.
14. The key idea of continuous batching is…
   A. Padding all sequences to the same length
   B. Waiting 5 ms to collect a full batch
   C. Making scheduling decisions every decode step, so sequences join and leave freely
   D. Running prefill and decode on different GPUs
   **Answer: C.** Iteration-level scheduling (Orca) keeps the batch full: finished sequences leave immediately and new ones join at the next step.
15. Long prompts arriving cause stream "freezes" for other users. What's the standard fix?
   A. Chunked prefill with a per-step token budget
   B. Raise temperature
   C. Disable the KV cache
   D. Use static batching
   **Answer: A.** Chunking spreads a long prefill over many steps, mixed with decodes, so inter-token latency stays smooth.
16. In vLLM, when KV memory runs out mid-generation, the default response is to…
   A. Crash with OOM
   B. Truncate the prompt
   C. Switch to CPU inference
   D. Preempt a sequence and recompute its KV later
   **Answer: D.** Preemption by recompute (or swapping to CPU) frees blocks. Frequent preemptions mean concurrency is set too high.
17. Static batching wastes GPU time mainly because…
   A. It can't use tensor cores
   B. Finished sequences sit idle until the longest one in the batch completes
   C. It requires FP32
   D. It doesn't support sampling
   **Answer: B.** The straggler problem: slots stay blocked by the slowest sequence, and new requests wait outside.
18. 64 query heads and 8 KV heads (GQA). How much smaller is the KV cache than MHA's?
   A. 2×
   B. 4×
   C. 8×
   D. 64×
   **Answer: C.** 64 ÷ 8 = 8× fewer K/V heads, so the cache is 8× smaller.
19. FlashAttention speeds up attention mainly by…
   A. Avoiding HBM reads/writes of the N×N score matrix through tiling in SRAM
   B. Approximating softmax with a polynomial
   C. Skipping distant tokens
   D. Using INT4 math
   **Answer: A.** It's IO-aware and exact. It tiles Q/K/V on-chip and uses online softmax, so the big matrix never touches HBM.
20. PagedAttention mainly solves which problem?
   A. Slow softmax
   B. KV-cache memory fragmentation and over-reservation
   C. Tokenizer speed
   D. Multi-GPU communication
   **Answer: B.** Fixed-size blocks plus a block table, like OS paging, cut KV waste from 60–80% to a few percent and allow block sharing.
21. Online softmax lets you compute softmax over a row…
   A. Only in FP32
   B. Without exponentials
   C. Approximately, with bounded error
   D. Chunk by chunk, keeping a running max and sum and rescaling
   **Answer: D.** When a larger max appears, the earlier partial sums are rescaled by exp(m_old − m_new). The result is exact.
22. At batch size 1, which scheme speeds up decode the most?
   A. W8A8 INT8
   B. W4A16 (4-bit weight-only)
   C. FP32 weights
   D. Quantizing only the LM head
   **Answer: B.** Batch 1 is purely memory-bound, so the fewest bytes per weight wins. Faster low-precision compute barely matters.
23. Why is per-group quantization (e.g. groups of 128) more accurate than per-tensor?
   A. It uses more bits per weight
   B. It skips the outliers
   C. Each group gets its own scale, so one large value only affects its own group
   D. It's done during training
   **Answer: C.** Finer scales follow local ranges. The cost is a little extra storage for the scales.
24. SmoothQuant makes W8A8 work by…
   A. Moving activation outliers into the weights with an equivalent per-channel rescale
   B. Keeping outliers in FP16
   C. Retraining the model
   D. Clipping all activations to ±1
   **Answer: A.** Divide activations and multiply weights by the same per-channel factor. The product is unchanged and both become easier to quantize.
25. Symmetric INT4 quantization has how many usable levels (with q_max = 7)?
   A. 4
   B. 8
   C. 16
   D. 15
   **Answer: D.** −7…+7 = 15 levels. (Full INT4 has 16 values, but the symmetric scheme usually leaves −8 unused.)
26. GPTQ improves on round-to-nearest by…
   A. Using larger groups
   B. Updating not-yet-quantized weights to compensate for each rounding error, using second-order info
   C. Fine-tuning with RL
   D. Quantizing activations first
   **Answer: B.** It quantizes column by column and uses Hessian information from calibration data to fix up the remaining columns.
27. With the proper acceptance rule, speculative decoding's outputs are…
   A. Distributed exactly like the target model's
   B. Slightly lower quality
   C. Identical to the draft model's
   D. Always greedy
   **Answer: A.** Rejection sampling (accept with min(1, p/q), else resample from max(0, p−q)) is lossless.
28. α = 0.8, k = 4 draft tokens. Expected tokens per target pass?
   A. 4.0
   B. 0.8
   C. ~3.36
   D. 5.0
   **Answer: C.** (1 − 0.8⁵) ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 0.672 ÷ 0.2 ≈ 3.36.
29. When does speculative decoding help least?
   A. Batch size 1, latency-sensitive chat
   B. Code editing with lots of repeated text
   C. Low-temperature structured output
   D. Very high batch sizes where the GPU is compute-bound
   **Answer: D.** When compute-bound, verifying extra tokens costs real FLOPs, and rejected drafts are wasted work.
30. Which parallelism reduces per-token latency for a model that already fits on one node?
   A. Data parallelism
   B. Tensor parallelism
   C. Pipeline parallelism
   D. More replicas
   **Answer: B.** TP splits each layer's weights, so every GPU reads only a fraction per step. PP and DP don't make a single token faster.
31. An MoE model has 671B total / 37B active parameters. Memory must hold…
   A. All 671B parameters
   B. Only the 37B active ones
   C. Only the router
   D. Half of the experts
   **Answer: A.** Any token can be routed to any expert, so all experts must be resident. Compute per token scales with the active parameters.
32. Expert parallelism mainly relies on which communication pattern?
   A. All-reduce
   B. Broadcast
   C. All-to-all
   D. No communication
   **Answer: C.** Tokens are dispatched to whichever GPUs hold their chosen experts, then combined back, both via all-to-all.
33. Your prompt template starts with the current timestamp. Effect on prefix caching?
   A. None
   B. Better hit rate
   C. Only TPOT changes
   D. The hit rate collapses, because the first block differs every request
   **Answer: D.** Block keys chain the whole prefix, so a change at the very start breaks every later match. Put dynamic content last.
34. Why does a block's cache key include its parent block's hash?
   A. To save memory
   B. Because KV depends on all preceding tokens, not just the block's own tokens
   C. For security
   D. To support FP8
   **Answer: B.** The same 16 tokens after a different prefix produce different KV. Chaining the hashes encodes the whole prefix.
35. The main benefit of prefill/decode disaggregation is…
   A. Removing interference, so TTFT and ITL can be tuned and scaled independently
   B. Smaller model weights
   C. No need for a KV cache
   D. Lower precision
   **Answer: A.** Separate pools stop prefills from stalling decodes. The cost is transferring the KV cache between them.
36. Which is the WORST autoscaling signal for an LLM server?
   A. Queue depth
   B. KV cache utilization
   C. CPU utilization
   D. p90 TTFT vs SLO
   **Answer: C.** The work happens on the GPU. CPU usage says almost nothing about inference capacity.
37. Why can pure "route to the best prefix-cache match" routing backfire?
   A. Cache hits are slower
   B. Popular prefixes overload one replica while others idle
   C. It breaks streaming
   D. It disables batching
   **Answer: B.** Good routers weigh cache overlap against current load.
38. Fusing RMSNorm with the residual add speeds things up because…
   A. It reduces FLOPs
   B. It enables FP4
   C. It improves accuracy
   D. It removes an HBM round-trip and a kernel launch for memory-bound ops
   **Answer: D.** Elementwise ops are memory-bound. Time follows bytes moved, and fusion moves fewer bytes.
39. CUDA graphs mainly help with…
   A. CPU kernel-launch overhead, especially in small-batch decode
   B. Large prefill FLOPs
   C. Model accuracy
   D. Network latency
   **Answer: A.** Hundreds of launches are replayed as one, so the GPU stops waiting on the CPU.
40. Why do engines capture CUDA graphs only for batch sizes like 1, 2, 4, 8…?
   A. GPUs only support powers of two
   B. Graphs require FP8
   C. Each graph has fixed shapes and costs memory and startup time, so engines pad to buckets
   D. Odd batch sizes are slower
   **Answer: C.** Padding to the next bucket wastes a little compute but keeps the number of graphs manageable.
41. You compute an MBU of 115%. What does that mean?
   A. Excellent kernels
   B. Your measurement or byte accounting is wrong
   C. The GPU is overclocked
   D. Prefix caching is off
   **Answer: B.** You can't beat peak bandwidth. Check the step timing, context lengths, and whether caching skipped work.
42. Your benchmark peaks at 9k tok/s, but p90 TPOT breaks the SLO above 6k tok/s. Your real capacity is…
   A. 9k tok/s
   B. 15k tok/s
   C. 7.5k tok/s
   D. ~6k tok/s
   **Answer: D.** Capacity is the highest load that still meets the SLO: the knee of the curve, not the peak.
43. Why must a server stop generating when a client disconnects?
   A. Otherwise the sequence keeps holding a batch slot, KV memory and GPU time for nobody
   B. HTTP requires it
   C. To keep logs small
   D. Tokenizers can't handle it
   **Answer: A.** Abandoned sequences take capacity away from real users.
44. Which load-testing style best reveals queueing collapse?
   A. Closed-loop with 1 user
   B. A single long request
   C. Open-loop: requests arrive at a target rate regardless of completions
   D. Running the same prompt 1000× with caching on
   **Answer: C.** Closed-loop load slows itself down when the server slows, which hides overload. Open-loop doesn't.
45. KV usage sits at 99% and preemptions are climbing. A reasonable first fix is…
   A. Raise max-num-seqs
   B. Lower max-num-seqs (or add replicas / use FP8 KV)
   C. Raise temperature
   D. Disable chunked prefill
   **Answer: B.** You're admitting more concurrent sequences than memory holds. Admit fewer, or make more room.
46. At temperature 0, an engine sometimes gives slightly different outputs for the same prompt. The most likely cause is…
   A. A bug in the tokenizer
   B. Random seeds
   C. Speculative decoding is lossy
   D. Batch composition changes floating-point reduction order
   **Answer: D.** Different batch shapes pick different kernels and summation orders, and tiny numeric differences can flip an argmax.

# Interview Prep

> Part of **InferenceLearn**, a free course on LLM inference engineering. Web version: interview.html. Whole course in one file: llms-full.txt

// boss rush

39 questions that come up in inference, ML-systems and LLM-infra interviews. Answer out loud first, then open the card and compare.

### How to use this page

- **Say your answer before opening the card.** Recognizing an answer is much easier than producing one.
- Strong answers follow a pattern: **name the bottleneck → do the napkin math → propose a fix → state the trade-off.**
- Levels: [junior] [mid] [senior] [staff]  are rough guides to depth, not hard rules.
- Practise with an AI: paste this page's link into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and ask it to interview you, one question at a time, and grade your answers.

## Fundamentals

**[junior] Walk me through what happens when an LLM serves one request.**

#### Strong answer

Tokenize the prompt. Run **prefill**: one forward pass over all prompt tokens in parallel, which fills the KV cache and produces logits for the first token. Sample a token, stream it back, then loop in **decode**: each step feeds one new token, appends its K/V to the cache, and samples the next, until EOS or max_tokens. Detokenize and stream as you go.

#### What they're testing

Whether you know the two phases and that decode is a sequential loop. Mentioning the KV cache unprompted is a good sign.

#### Follow-ups

- Which phase dominates latency for a 2k-in / 500-out chat request? (Decode: 500 sequential steps.)
- Where does the scheduler fit in?

**[mid] Why do prefill and decode stress the GPU so differently?**

#### Strong answer

Prefill multiplies the weights by a matrix of N prompt tokens, so each weight byte loaded is reused N times. Arithmetic intensity is high and it's **compute-bound**. Decode multiplies the weights by one vector per sequence, so it's about 1 FLOP per byte at batch 1 and **memory-bandwidth-bound**. Decode also reads the KV cache, which can't be shared across sequences.

#### What they're testing

The roofline intuition, which most of inference optimization rests on.

#### Follow-ups

- How does batching change decode's position on the roofline?
- What is attention's intensity in decode, and why doesn't batching help it?

**[junior] Greedy vs temperature vs top-p sampling: when would you use each?**

#### Strong answer

Greedy (T=0) for deterministic tasks such as extraction, classification and code where you want the most likely answer. Temperature 0.7–1.0 with top-p ≈ 0.9–0.95 for creative or chat output. Top-p adapts the candidate set to the model's confidence, while top-k is a fixed cutoff. Mention that sampling has a cost in serving (sorting large vocabularies per sequence), so engines use fused GPU samplers.

#### What they're testing

Basic decoding knowledge plus some awareness of the systems side.

#### Follow-ups

- Why can T=0 still be non-deterministic in a batched server?

**[mid] Estimate the max single-user tokens/s for a 70B model in FP8 on one H200.**

#### Strong answer

The weights are ~70 GB in FP8. H200 bandwidth is ~4.8 TB/s, so each step takes ≥ 70 / 4800 s ≈ 14.6 ms, or about **68 tok/s** at the speed of light. Expect ~70–85% of that in practice, and less at long context because KV reads add bytes.

#### What they're testing

Whether you can do speed-of-light math quickly and know that bandwidth is the limit.

#### Follow-ups

- How does this change with TP=2 on two GPUs? (Roughly halves bytes per GPU per step, minus communication overhead.)
- And with batch 64?

**[senior] A new GPU doubles FLOPs but only raises bandwidth 1.3×. What happens to LLM serving performance?**

#### Strong answer

Low-batch decode speeds up by only ~1.3× because it's bandwidth-bound. Prefill and large-batch decode can gain up to ~2× if the kernels use the new compute. The ridge point rises (FLOPs ÷ BW goes up ~1.5×), so you need *bigger* batches to reach compute-bound. That pushes you toward larger batches, lower precision (to cut bytes), speculative decoding (to turn spare FLOPs into tokens), and disaggregation (to put prefill on the compute-rich parts).

#### What they're testing

Applying roofline reasoning to hardware trends.

#### Follow-ups

- Which optimizations become *more* valuable on that GPU?

**[junior] Define TTFT, TPOT and throughput. Which matters most for a chatbot vs a batch summarization job?**

#### Strong answer

TTFT = time to first token (queue + prefill). TPOT = average time per output token after the first. Throughput = total tokens/s across all users. A chatbot cares about TTFT (does it feel responsive?) and a TPOT faster than reading speed. Offline batch jobs care almost only about throughput and cost, so you can use huge batches and accept high latency.

#### What they're testing

That optimization goals depend on the product.

#### Follow-ups

- Why report p99 rather than the mean?
- What is goodput?

**[mid] How would you benchmark two inference engines fairly?**

#### Strong answer

Same model, precision, hardware and parallelism. A realistic input/output length distribution. Fixed output lengths (ignore_eos) so both engines do the same work. Warm up first. Use open-loop arrivals and sweep the request rate. Measure TTFT/ITL percentiles at the client with streaming. Compare throughput **at equal latency SLOs**, not peak throughput. Control prefix caching. Report versions and flags.

#### What they're testing

Experimental rigor. Lots of published benchmarks are misleading.

#### Follow-ups

- Why is closed-loop testing misleading near saturation?

**[mid] Your API serves 40 req/s, each ~10 s end to end. How much KV memory do you need for an 8B model (128 KiB/token) at ~2k tokens per request?**

#### Strong answer

Little's law: 40 × 10 = 400 concurrent requests. Each holds ~2k × 128 KiB = 256 MiB of KV, so ~100 GiB in total. That doesn't fit next to the weights on one 80 GB GPU, so you need at least two replicas, more with headroom. Prefix caching or FP8 KV could cut it.

#### What they're testing

Linking traffic to memory with napkin math.

#### Follow-ups

- What if average output length doubles?

## Memory & batching

**[junior] What is the KV cache and why does it exist?**

#### Strong answer

With causal attention, each past token's key and value vectors never change once computed. Caching them means each decode step computes K/V only for the new token and attends over the cache. That turns quadratic recomputation into linear work. The cost is memory that grows with layers × KV heads × head dim × sequence length × batch.

#### What they're testing

The most fundamental concept in serving.

#### Follow-ups

- Why aren't queries cached?
- Compute the per-token size for Llama-3-8B.

**[mid] Why is serving 128k-token contexts so much more expensive than 4k?**

#### Strong answer

(1) KV memory grows linearly, so 32× more per sequence and far fewer sequences per GPU, which means lower throughput and higher cost. (2) Every decode step reads the whole cache. At long context, KV bytes can exceed weight bytes, and batching doesn't amortize them. (3) Prefill attention is O(N²) compute, so TTFT grows a lot. (4) Scheduling gets harder: big preemptions and big prefills that stall other users.

#### What they're testing

A view of all the dimensions of long-context cost.

#### Follow-ups

- What mitigations exist? (GQA/MLA, FP8 KV, prefix caching, context parallelism, sliding windows.)

**[senior] You're out of KV memory at your target concurrency. List options in order of what you'd try.**

#### Strong answer

(1) Check config: `gpu-memory-utilization`, an over-sized `max-model-len`, CUDA-graph memory. (2) Enable prefix caching if prompts share prefixes. (3) FP8 KV cache, about 2× capacity with small quality risk, so evaluate it. (4) Quantize the weights to free memory for KV. (5) Add TP to pool memory, or add replicas. (6) Offload cold KV to CPU. (7) Long term, pick a model with a smaller KV footprint (GQA/MLA). Each step trades cost, quality or latency.

#### What they're testing

Practical prioritization: cheap, safe changes first.

#### Follow-ups

- How would you validate that FP8 KV didn't hurt quality?

**[junior] Explain continuous batching and why it beats static batching.**

#### Strong answer

Static batching runs a fixed batch until its longest sequence finishes, so short sequences leave idle slots and new requests wait. Continuous (iteration-level) batching re-decides the batch every decode step: finished sequences leave immediately and waiting ones join. The GPU stays full, often giving several times more throughput at similar latency. It needs ragged-batch kernels and paged KV memory.

#### What they're testing

The core scheduling idea behind every modern engine.

#### Follow-ups

- What new problem does it create? (Prefill/decode interference.)

**[mid] What is chunked prefill, and how do you tune it?**

#### Strong answer

Split long prompts into chunks and fill each step's token budget with decode tokens first, then a prefill chunk. This stops long prefills from freezing everyone's token stream, and it mixes compute-heavy and memory-heavy work in the same step. The knob is the per-step token budget (e.g. max-num-batched-tokens): smaller gives smoother ITL but slower TTFT for long prompts; larger gives better throughput and TTFT but spikier ITL.

#### What they're testing

Understanding the latency trade-off, not just the definition.

#### Follow-ups

- How does this compare with disaggregation?

**[senior] Preemption: recompute vs swap. When is each better?**

#### Strong answer

Recompute throws away the victim's KV and re-runs prefill later. Its cost is compute, and prefill is fast and parallel, so it's cheap for short contexts. Swap copies the KV to CPU and back. Its cost is PCIe bandwidth (~tens of GB/s) and CPU memory. For long contexts where recompute is expensive, or on systems with fast CPU–GPU links (e.g. NVLink-C2C), swapping can win. In both cases, frequent preemption means you're over-admitting: fix the admission limits.

#### What they're testing

Reasoning about costs on different resources.

#### Follow-ups

- Which sequence would you choose as the victim, and why?

## Attention & quantization

**[mid] How does FlashAttention work, and is it an approximation?**

#### Strong answer

It's exact. Naive attention writes the N×N score matrix to HBM and reads it back for softmax and the V product, so it's memory-bound. FlashAttention tiles Q/K/V into SRAM, computes partial scores per tile, and combines them with **online softmax** (running max and sum, rescaling). Only the output goes to HBM. Memory traffic drops from O(N²) to O(N), giving big speedups and allowing long sequences.

#### What they're testing

IO-awareness, the most important performance idea of recent years.

#### Follow-ups

- Derive the online-softmax update.
- What did FA2 and FA3 change?

**[mid] What problem does PagedAttention solve, and what else does it enable?**

#### Strong answer

Contiguous per-request KV reservations waste memory through over-reservation and fragmentation; the vLLM paper measured 60–80% waste in earlier systems. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks mapped by a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory, so waste is under ~4%. It also enables **sharing** via reference counts and copy-on-write: parallel sampling, beam search and prefix caching.

#### What they're testing

Memory management as a throughput lever.

#### Follow-ups

- How does block size affect performance and waste?

**[senior] Compare MHA, GQA and MLA from a serving perspective.**

#### Strong answer

MHA has one KV head per query head: the largest cache and the lowest decode-attention intensity. GQA shares KV heads across groups of query heads: g× smaller cache, g× more reuse per byte, and near-MHA quality, which is why it's the default. MLA caches a low-rank latent per token and absorbs the projections at inference: a much smaller cache, but different kernels, and some wrinkles with TP sharding and positional embeddings. All three change how many sequences fit, and so throughput.

#### What they're testing

Connecting architecture to memory, bandwidth and parallelism.

#### Follow-ups

- Why does a small number of KV heads limit the tensor-parallel degree?

**[mid] W4A16 vs W8A8 (FP8): when would you choose each?**

#### Strong answer

W4A16 cuts weight bytes 4× and is ideal for memory-bound, low-batch serving or fitting big models on small GPUs. The math still runs in BF16 with dequantization overhead, so it can lose at high batch. W8A8 (FP8 on Hopper) halves bytes *and* uses faster FP8 tensor cores, so it helps prefill and high-batch throughput too, and it's usually near-lossless. Rule of thumb: FP8 for throughput serving on modern GPUs; INT4 weight-only for latency at low concurrency or tight memory.

#### What they're testing

Matching quantization to the bottleneck.

#### Follow-ups

- Where would FP8 KV cache fit in?

**[senior] Why are activations harder to quantize than weights, and how do people deal with it?**

#### Strong answer

Activations vary per input and contain systematic outlier channels 10–100× larger than the rest. Per-tensor INT8 scaling then crushes the normal values. Fixes: mixed precision for outliers (LLM.int8), SmoothQuant (migrate scale into the weights), per-token dynamic scales, rotations (QuaRot/SpinQuant) to spread outliers, and FP8, whose exponent handles range better than INT8.

#### What they're testing

Depth beyond "just use INT8".

#### Follow-ups

- Static vs dynamic activation scales: what's the trade-off?

**[mid] How would you decide a quantized model is safe to ship?**

#### Strong answer

Perplexity as a smoke test only. Then task evals matching the product (knowledge, math, code, long-context retrieval, multilingual if relevant) plus a domain eval set. Side-by-side human or LLM-judge comparisons on real traffic samples. Check the tails: math and code break first. Measure the actual speed and cost gain at the production batch size. Then canary-deploy with quality metrics.

#### What they're testing

Evaluation discipline.

#### Follow-ups

- A 0.5% MMLU drop: ship or not? (Depends on the product and what it saves.)

## Speculative decoding & parallelism

**[mid] Explain speculative decoding and why it doesn't change the output distribution.**

#### Strong answer

A cheap drafter proposes k tokens and the target verifies all of them in one forward pass, which costs about one decode step when memory-bound. Accept draft token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). On the first rejection, resample from normalize(max(0, p − q)) and stop. This rejection-sampling scheme provably yields samples from p. Expected tokens per pass = (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α).

#### What they're testing

Both the systems intuition and the probability argument.

#### Follow-ups

- What's the greedy special case?
- What happens to the KV cache for rejected tokens?

**[senior] Speculative decoding made p50 latency better but throughput worse under load. Why, and what would you do?**

#### Strong answer

At high batch the engine is compute-bound. Verifying k extra tokens per sequence adds real FLOPs, and rejected drafts are pure waste, so total throughput drops. Options: adapt k (or turn speculation off) based on batch size or load; use cheaper drafters (n-gram, EAGLE heads); only speculate for latency-sensitive tiers; and track acceptance rate per workload.

#### What they're testing

Knowing when an optimization stops paying off.

#### Follow-ups

- Which metrics would you put on a dashboard for this?

**[junior] Name three ways to get draft tokens.**

#### Strong answer

A small draft model from the same family (same tokenizer); n-gram or prompt-lookup copying from the context; extra prediction heads trained on the target (Medusa, EAGLE) or built-in MTP modules (e.g. DeepSeek-V3).

#### What they're testing

Breadth.

#### Follow-ups

- Which would you pick for a code-editing product, and why? (Prompt lookup: edits copy large spans.)

**[mid] Tensor vs pipeline parallelism for inference: trade-offs?**

#### Strong answer

TP splits each layer across GPUs. It cuts per-token latency, since each GPU reads 1/N of the weights, but needs two all-reduces per layer, so it wants NVLink within a node. PP splits layers into stages, with cheap point-to-point communication that works across nodes. It doesn't reduce single-token latency and needs many micro-batches to avoid bubbles. The usual setup is TP inside a node and PP across nodes, then data-parallel replicas for throughput.

#### What they're testing

Understanding which parallelism reduces latency and which only adds capacity.

#### Follow-ups

- Why does TP stop scaling well beyond 8 GPUs?

**[senior] What makes serving large MoE models hard?**

#### Strong answer

Memory scales with total parameters but compute with active ones, so you need lots of memory and little compute per token. At high batch, nearly all experts are touched every step, so weight reads aren't small anymore. Expert parallelism needs all-to-all dispatch and combine, which is latency-sensitive. Load imbalance creates hot experts and stragglers. Fixes include wide EP with attention data parallelism, redundant hot experts, specialized all-to-all kernels, grouped GEMMs, and overlapping communication with compute.

#### What they're testing

Current frontier knowledge.

#### Follow-ups

- Why might you pair attention data parallelism with expert parallelism?

**[staff] Estimate the tensor-parallel all-reduce traffic per decode step for a 70B dense model, batch 64, TP=8.**

#### Strong answer

With hidden size ~8192 and 80 layers, there are 2 all-reduces per layer, each on a [64 × 8192] BF16 tensor = 1 MiB. That's 160 all-reduces of ~1 MiB per step, and a ring all-reduce moves ~2·(N−1)/N × size per GPU ≈ 1.75 MiB each, so ~280 MiB per GPU per step. At ~450 GB/s effective NVLink that's ~0.6 ms of bandwidth time. But 160 small collectives each carry latency (tens of µs), so **latency, not bandwidth,** often dominates. Hence fused all-reduce kernels, overlap, and custom one-shot all-reduce for small messages.

#### What they're testing

Quantitative distributed-systems reasoning.

#### Follow-ups

- How does this change for prefill with 8k tokens?

## Serving systems

**[mid] How would you implement prefix caching in a paged-KV engine?**

#### Strong answer

Give each full block a key = hash(parent key, the block's token IDs, extras like LoRA ID). Keep a hash → physical-block map. On a new request, hash the prompt block by block, reuse the longest run of hits (incrementing ref counts), and prefill from there. When a request finishes, its blocks go to an evictable LRU list rather than being freed. Evict only blocks with ref count 0, leaves first. The alternative is a radix tree (SGLang) for token-level matching.

#### What they're testing

Data-structure design under memory pressure.

#### Follow-ups

- How do you handle a partially filled last block?
- Hash collisions?

**[senior] You run 20 replicas behind a round-robin load balancer and prefix-cache hit rates are poor. What do you change?**

#### Strong answer

Round-robin scatters each conversation across replicas, so caches never warm up. Move to cache-aware routing: session affinity (hash the conversation ID) as a cheap first step, then a KV-aware router that scores replicas on predicted prefix overlap minus current load, to avoid hotspots. Also fix the prompt template so static content comes first, and consider a shared or offloaded KV tier.

#### What they're testing

Seeing the system as a whole beyond one engine.

#### Follow-ups

- How do you measure success? (Hit rate, TTFT and GPU prefill time per request.)

**[senior] When is prefill/decode disaggregation worth it, and what does it cost?**

#### Strong answer

It's worth it at scale with strict, separate TTFT and ITL SLOs, long prompts, or very different prefill and decode loads. Separate pools remove interference and can be scaled and configured independently. Costs: KV transfer bandwidth (e.g. ~640 MB for 2k tokens on a 70B GQA model, needing RDMA or NVLink), extra operational complexity, new failure modes, and possible stranded capacity if the pool ratio is wrong. For small deployments, chunked prefill on one pool is usually enough.

#### What they're testing

Judging when an architecture pays off.

#### Follow-ups

- How would you choose the prefill:decode GPU ratio?

**[mid] What signals would you autoscale an LLM service on?**

#### Strong answer

Queue depth or waiting requests, KV-cache utilization, TTFT/ITL percentiles against the SLO, and tokens/s against benchmarked capacity. Not CPU, and not raw nvidia-smi utilization. Account for slow cold starts (weights, compilation, graph capture) with warm pools, local weight caches and predictive scaling.

#### What they're testing

Production operations knowledge.

#### Follow-ups

- How do you scale down without dropping streams? (Graceful drain.)

**[staff] Design a scheduler that serves interactive and batch traffic on the same GPUs.**

#### Strong answer

Use priority classes: interactive requests are admitted first and their decodes always get budget, with a guaranteed TTFT/ITL target. Batch requests fill leftover token budget and are preemptible (recompute preferred, since they're latency-tolerant). Use admission control per class, fairness across tenants within a class (token-based fair queueing), and maybe a different speculation policy per class. Monitor goodput for interactive traffic and throughput and cost for batch. Scale on interactive SLO signals and let batch traffic soak up idle capacity.

#### What they're testing

Policy design with competing objectives.

#### Follow-ups

- How do you prevent starvation of batch jobs?

## Kernels & production

**[mid] What are CUDA graphs and why do inference engines use them?**

#### Strong answer

They record a sequence of kernel launches with fixed shapes and addresses, then replay it with one launch. Small-batch decode steps are short (milliseconds) but launch hundreds of kernels, so CPU launch overhead can rival GPU time. Graphs remove it. Engines capture one graph per batch-size bucket and pad up, mostly for decode. The costs are capture time, memory, and rigid shapes.

#### What they're testing

Understanding CPU vs GPU overheads.

#### Follow-ups

- Why aren't graphs typically used for prefill?

**[mid] Give an example of kernel fusion in an LLM and explain the speedup.**

#### Strong answer

SwiGLU: silu(gate) × up. Unfused, it's separate kernels that each read and write the full [tokens × 14336] tensors to HBM. Fused, it's one read of each input and one write of the output. Elementwise work is memory-bound, so time drops roughly in proportion to the bytes saved, plus launches. Other examples: RMSNorm+residual(+FP8 quant), rotary fused into attention, dequant fused into GEMM.

#### What they're testing

Bytes-moved reasoning at the kernel level.

#### Follow-ups

- Sketch that kernel in Triton.

**[senior] A decode step takes 2× longer than your speed-of-light estimate. How do you find out why?**

#### Strong answer

First check the estimate itself: include KV bytes at the actual context lengths and the communication. Then take an Nsight Systems trace and look for gaps between kernels (CPU-bound: scheduling, sampling sync, Python, missing CUDA graphs), many tiny kernels (missing fusion), and slow collectives. Then use Nsight Compute on the top kernels for achieved bandwidth vs peak, occupancy and wave quantization. Compute MBU per kernel class and fix the biggest gap first.

#### What they're testing

A systematic performance-debugging method.

#### Follow-ups

- Which GEMM shapes in decode tend to underutilize the GPU?

**[mid] p99 latency doubled after a deploy. Walk me through the investigation.**

#### Strong answer

Is it TTFT or ITL? Check queue depth and running sequences (a capacity problem?), KV usage and preemptions, and prefix-cache hit rate (did a prompt template change?). Diff the deploy: engine version, flags (token budget, max seqs, speculation), model or precision. Check the traffic mix (longer prompts?). Look for hardware issues (a straggler GPU, throttling). Roll back if the SLO is breached, then bisect.

#### What they're testing

Calm, data-driven incident response.

#### Follow-ups

- Which three dashboards do you open first?

**[senior] How do you plan capacity for a new LLM feature?**

#### Strong answer

Gather peak req/s, input and output length distributions, and SLOs. Napkin math: token demand, Little's-law concurrency, KV memory, and whether the model fits with headroom. Benchmark one replica on realistic data and find the knee where p90 still meets the SLO. Replicas = demand ÷ knee capacity, plus headroom for spikes, failures and deploys (N+1, ~30%). Validate with an open-loop load test at 1.5× peak, then set autoscaling signals.

#### What they're testing

Turning product requirements into infrastructure.

#### Follow-ups

- What changes if 60% of the input tokens are a shared system prompt?

## System design (open-ended)

**[staff] Design an API that serves a 70B chat model at 500 req/s with p90 TTFT < 1 s and TPOT < 40 ms.**

#### A strong structure

- **Requirements:** lengths (say 2k in / 400 out), streaming, multi-tenancy, availability target.
- **Napkin math:** 500 × 400 = 200k output tok/s. Concurrency ≈ 500 × (~1 + 400×0.035 ≈ 15 s) ≈ 7,500 sequences. KV ≈ 7,500 × 2.4k tokens × 320 KiB ≈ 5.5 TiB, so hundreds of GPUs. FP8 weights and KV halve it.
- **Replica design:** FP8, TP=4 or 8 on H100/H200 nodes, continuous batching with chunked prefill, prefix caching, CUDA graphs. Benchmark the knee per replica.
- **Fleet:** KV/prefix-aware router, autoscaling on queue depth and SLOs, warm pools, multi-region.
- **At this scale, consider:** P/D disaggregation, speculative decoding for the latency tier.
- **Operations:** rate limits, max-token caps, cancellation, observability, canaries, rollback.

#### What they're testing

Driving a design from numbers, and making trade-offs explicit.

**[staff] Design serving for a RAG product: 30k-token prompts (mostly retrieved docs), short answers.**

#### A strong structure

- **Prefill-dominated:** TTFT and prefill compute are the cost drivers, not decode.
- **Reuse:** cache KV for popular documents. Order prompts as [system][docs sorted by a stable ID][question]. Use a KV offload tier (CPU/SSD) for document caches. Route on document overlap.
- **Compute:** FP8 prefill, high-TP or disaggregated prefill pools, chunked prefill so the few decoders aren't starved.
- **Memory:** long KV per request but short lifetimes. Size the pool for burst concurrency.
- **Product lever:** retrieve fewer and better chunks. The cheapest token is the one you never send.

#### What they're testing

Recognizing the workload shape and optimizing for it.

**[staff] Design a platform where 1,000 customers each have their own fine-tuned variant of one 8B base model.**

#### A strong structure

- Don't deploy 1,000 full models. Use **LoRA adapters** on a shared base with multi-LoRA batching (kernels that apply different adapters per sequence in one batch).
- Keep adapters in GPU memory with LRU caching, a CPU/SSD tier behind it, and preloading for hot tenants.
- Prefix-cache keys must include the adapter ID.
- Routing: send a tenant's requests to replicas with the adapter loaded, balanced against load.
- Per-tenant fairness, rate limits and usage metering. Isolation for noisy neighbours.
- Trade-off: high-rank adapters or full fine-tunes for the top customers might justify dedicated replicas.

#### What they're testing

Multi-tenancy, caching hierarchies and cost awareness.

# Workbook

> Part of **InferenceLearn**, a free course on LLM inference engineering. Web version: workbook.html. Whole course in one file: llms-full.txt

// grind zone

Deep understanding comes from working things out yourself. Try each problem on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the solution.

### Your cheat sheet

| Forward-pass FLOPs | ≈ 2 × params per token |
|---|---|
| Decode step (memory-bound) | ≥ (weight bytes + KV bytes) ÷ bandwidth |
| Prefill time | ≥ 2 × params × tokens ÷ (peak FLOP/s × MFU) |
| KV per token | 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes |
| Linear-layer intensity (BF16) | ≈ batch size, in FLOP/byte |
| Little's law | concurrency = throughput × latency |
| Speculative decoding | E[tokens] = (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α) |
| H100 SXM (approx.) | 989 TFLOPS BF16 dense · 3.35 TB/s · 80 GB · ridge ≈ 295 |

## Part 1: Napkin-math problems

[World 1]

[warm-up]

### P1 · How long is that answer?

**Given:** the model writes a 600-word answer. 1 token ≈ 0.75 words. TTFT = 400 ms, TPOT = 25 ms.  
**Find:** output tokens and total response time.

**Hint**

Convert words to tokens first, then use E2E = TTFT + TPOT × (tokens − 1).

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Tokens = 600 ÷ 0.75 = **800 tokens**.
2. Decode time = 25 ms × 799 ≈ 20.0 s.
3. E2E = 0.4 + 20.0 ≈ **20.4 s**.

**Takeaway:** long answers are almost entirely decode time. Shaving TPOT matters far more than TTFT here.

[World 1]

[roofline]

### P2 · Speed of light on an A100

**Given:** Llama-3-8B, A100 80GB (2.04 TB/s), batch 1.  
**Find:** max decode tok/s in BF16, and in INT4 weight-only.

**Hint**

At batch 1, step time ≈ weight bytes ÷ bandwidth. How many bytes per parameter in each format?

**Step-by-step solution**

1. BF16: 8e9 × 2 = 16 GB → 16 ÷ 2040 s ≈ 7.8 ms → **~128 tok/s**.
2. INT4: 8e9 × 0.5 = 4 GB → ≈ 1.96 ms → **~510 tok/s** (in theory).
3. Reality: dequantization overhead, KV reads and launch overheads mean INT4 usually gives ~2–3×, not 4×.

**Takeaway:** at batch 1, bytes per weight is the speed dial.

[World 1]

[roofline]

### P3 · When does decode become compute-bound?

**Given:** H100: 989 TFLOPS BF16, ~1979 TFLOPS FP8 (dense), 3.35 TB/s.  
**Find:** the batch size where linear layers become compute-bound for (a) BF16 weights and compute, (b) FP8 weights and compute.

**Hint**

Intensity = 2·P·B ÷ (P × bytes per param). Set it equal to the ridge point for each precision.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. (a) Ridge = 989 ÷ 3.35 ≈ 295. Intensity = 2B ÷ 2 = B, so **B ≈ 295**.
2. (b) Ridge = 1979 ÷ 3.35 ≈ 591. Intensity = 2B ÷ 1 = 2B, so 2B = 591 and **B ≈ 295** again!
3. FP8 doubles both the FLOPs and the work per byte, so the crossover batch stays the same, but every step is ~2× faster.

**Takeaway:** real batches are usually smaller than ~300 (KV memory limits them), so decode is memory-bound in most deployments.

[World 1]

[prefill]

### P4 · TTFT for a long prompt

**Given:** 70B dense model, 8,192-token prompt, 8×H100 with TP=8, 50% MFU.  
**Find:** approximate prefill time (ignore the extra attention FLOPs).

**Hint**

Total FLOPs = 2 × params × tokens. Divide by the cluster's effective FLOP/s.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. FLOPs = 2 × 70e9 × 8192 ≈ 1.15e15.
2. Effective compute = 8 × 989e12 × 0.5 ≈ 3.96e15 FLOP/s.
3. Time ≈ 1.15e15 ÷ 3.96e15 ≈ **0.29 s**. Attention adds more at long context.

**Takeaway:** prefill scales with prompt length × params. Prefix caching avoids paying it twice.

[World 2]

[KV cache]

### P5 · The price of long context

**Given:** Llama-3-70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, BF16 KV.  
**Find:** KV per token, and per 32k-token sequence. What does FP8 KV change?

**Hint**

2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Per token = 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 B = **320 KiB**.
2. Per 32k sequence = 320 KiB × 32,768 = **10 GiB**.
3. FP8 KV halves it to 5 GiB, so twice as many concurrent long-context users fit.

**Takeaway:** one long-context user can need as much memory as a small model's entire weights.

[World 2]

[memory budget]

### P6 · Will it fit on a 24 GB card?

**Given:** Qwen2.5-7B (~7.6B params; 28 layers, 4 KV heads, head dim 128) on a 24 GB GPU, 90% usable, ~1.5 GB workspace.  
**Find:** how many KV tokens fit with BF16 weights vs INT4 weights (~0.5 B/param)?

**Hint**

KV room = usable − weights − workspace. Then divide by KV bytes per token.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Usable = 21.6 GB. KV per token = 2 × 28 × 4 × 128 × 2 = 57,344 B = 56 KiB.
2. BF16 weights ≈ 15.2 GB → room = 21.6 − 15.2 − 1.5 = 4.9 GB → ≈ **85k tokens** (about 10 × 8k-token chats).
3. INT4 weights ≈ 3.8 GB → room ≈ 16.3 GB → ≈ **284k tokens**, about 3.3× more concurrent users.

**Takeaway:** on small GPUs, quantizing the weights mainly buys KV capacity, which means throughput.

[World 2]

[batching]

### P7 · Static vs continuous by hand

**Given:** 2 slots. Requests arrive in order R0..R3 needing 8, 2, 2 and 8 decode steps.  
**Find:** total steps and slot utilization for static batching (pairs in order) vs continuous batching (fill the earliest-free slot).

**Hint**

Draw a 2-row grid and fill it in. Useful work = 8+2+2+8 = 20 slot-steps.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Static: batch {R0,R1} takes max(8,2) = 8 steps, batch {R2,R3} takes 8 → **16 steps**, utilization 20 ÷ 32 = 62.5%.
2. Continuous: slot A runs R0 (0–8). Slot B runs R1 (0–2), R2 (2–4), R3 (4–12) → **12 steps**, utilization 20 ÷ 24 = 83%.
3. A perfect packing would take 10 steps. Arrival order still matters, which is why some schedulers consider predicted lengths.

**Takeaway:** continuous batching removes the straggler waste. Try more cases in the [simulator](lessons/05-batching.md).

[World 2]

[quantization]

### P8 · Quantize four numbers by hand

**Given:** weights [0.10, −0.30, 0.05, 2.40], symmetric INT4 (q_max = 7).  
**Find:** the dequantized values with (a) one per-tensor scale, (b) per-group scales with groups of 2.

**Hint**

s = max|x| ÷ 7, q = round(x ÷ s), x̂ = q × s.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. (a) s = 2.4 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.343. q = [0, −1, 0, 7], so x̂ = [**0**, −0.343, **0**, 2.40]. Two weights wiped out!
2. (b) Group 1 [0.10, −0.30]: s = 0.3 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.0429, q = [2, −7], x̂ = [0.086, −0.300].
3. Group 2 [0.05, 2.40]: s ≈ 0.343, q = [0, 7], x̂ = [0, 2.40]. Only the weight sharing a group with the outlier suffers.

**Takeaway:** outliers stretch the scale, and smaller groups contain the damage. See it live in the [quantization playground](lessons/07-quantization.md).

[World 3]

[speculative]

### P9 · Choosing the draft length

**Given:** acceptance rate α = 0.7. Each draft token costs 0.1 of a target forward pass.  
**Find:** the ideal speedup for k = 3 and k = 6. Which is better?

**Hint**

Speedup = E[tokens] ÷ (1 + k × 0.1).

**Step-by-step solution**

1. k=3: E = (1 − 0.7⁴) ÷ 0.3 = 0.7599 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 2.53. Cost = 1.3. Speedup ≈ **1.95×**.
2. k=6: E = (1 − 0.7⁷) ÷ 0.3 = 0.9176 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.06. Cost = 1.6. Speedup ≈ **1.91×**.
3. k=3 wins slightly. Tokens far down the chain are rarely accepted but always cost drafting time.

**Takeaway:** the best k grows with α and shrinks with draft cost.

[World 3]

[parallelism]

### P10 · Does TP=8 halve latency vs TP=4?

**Given:** 70B BF16, decode at small batch on H100s. 80 layers × 2 all-reduces per layer, ~20 µs each (latency-dominated).  
**Find:** step time at TP=4 and TP=8.

**Hint**

The number of all-reduces per step doesn't depend on the TP size. Only the weight bytes per GPU do.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Communication = 160 × 20 µs = 3.2 ms per step, in both cases.
2. TP=4: 140 GB ÷ 4 = 35 GB per GPU → 10.4 ms → total ≈ **13.6 ms**.
3. TP=8: 17.5 GB → 5.2 ms → total ≈ **8.4 ms**. That's 1.6× faster, not 2×.

**Takeaway:** fixed communication latency limits TP scaling. Hence fused, low-latency all-reduce kernels.

[World 3]

[prefix caching]

### P11 · What is prefix caching worth?

**Given:** 8B model, 3,000-token shared system prompt + 500-token user part, 1M requests/day, 90% cache hits, H100 at 50% MFU, $3/GPU-hour.  
**Find:** GPU-hours of prefill saved per day.

**Hint**

Saved tokens = hit rate × shared tokens × requests. FLOPs = 2 × params × tokens.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Saved tokens = 0.9 × 3,000 × 1M = 2.7e9 tokens/day.
2. FLOPs = 2 × 8e9 × 2.7e9 ≈ 4.3e19.
3. Effective H100 = 0.5 × 989e12 ≈ 4.9e14 FLOP/s → ≈ 87,000 s ≈ **24 GPU-hours/day** (≈ $72/day), plus much lower TTFT (prefill 500 tokens instead of 3,500).

**Takeaway:** stable prompt prefixes are free money. Design templates for caching.

[World 3]

[disaggregation]

### P12 · Is KV transfer a deal-breaker?

**Given:** 8B model (128 KiB/token KV), 4,096-token prompt. Network 25 GB/s (≈200 Gb/s) or 100 GB/s. Prefill on one H100 at 50% MFU.  
**Find:** KV transfer time vs prefill time.

**Hint**

KV bytes = tokens × per-token size.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. KV = 4096 × 128 KiB = 512 MiB ≈ 0.54 GB.
2. Transfer: ≈ 21 ms at 25 GB/s, ≈ 5.4 ms at 100 GB/s.
3. Prefill ≈ 2 × 8e9 × 4096 ÷ (0.5 × 989e12) ≈ 132 ms. So transfer adds ~16% at 25 GB/s and ~4% at 100 GB/s, and layer-by-layer streaming can hide much of it.

**Takeaway:** disaggregation needs fast links. Small models with long prompts make the trade-off the tightest.

[World 4]

[profiling]

### P13 · Compute your MBU

**Given:** 8B BF16 model, batch 16, average context 4k tokens, measured decode step 8 ms on H100.  
**Find:** bytes per step, achieved bandwidth, and MBU.

**Hint**

Bytes = weights + KV for every sequence.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Weights = 16 GB. KV = 16 × 4096 × 128 KiB = 8 GiB ≈ 8.6 GB. Total ≈ 24.6 GB.
2. Achieved = 24.6 GB ÷ 8 ms ≈ 3.07 TB/s.
3. MBU = 3.07 ÷ 3.35 ≈ **92%**. Suspiciously high: double-check the context lengths and timing before celebrating.

**Takeaway:** MBU tells you how much speed is left. Over ~90% usually means a measurement mistake.

[World 4]

[capacity]

### P14 · Fleet size and cost

**Given:** 5M requests/day, 400 output tokens each, peak traffic = 3× average, benchmarked knee = 3,000 output tok/s per GPU, 30% headroom, $3/GPU-hour.  
**Find:** peak GPU count, and $/1M tokens for a static fleet vs perfect autoscaling.

**Hint**

Average tok/s = requests × tokens ÷ 86,400. Size for the peak, then compare with what you actually use.

**Step-by-step solution**

1. Average = 5e6 × 400 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,100 tok/s. Peak ≈ 69,400 tok/s.
2. Peak GPUs = 69,400 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 23.1, plus 30% → **~31 GPUs**.
3. Static fleet: 31 × $3 × 24 = $2,232/day for 2,000M tokens → **$1.12 per 1M**.
4. Autoscaling at average load: 23,100 ÷ 3,000 × 1.3 ≈ 10 GPUs → ~$720/day → **~$0.36 per 1M**.

**Takeaway:** utilization can matter as much as kernel speed. Idle GPUs are the most expensive ones.

## Part 2: Explain it back (Feynman checks)

If you can explain something simply, you understand it. Answer each one out loud in under a minute, without notes. Then check against the lesson, or ask an AI tutor to grade you.

1. Explain to a non-engineer why a chatbot's first word takes longer than each word after it.
2. Explain why making the GPU's math twice as fast doesn't make single-user chat twice as fast.
3. Explain the KV cache using the analogy of taking notes in a meeting.
4. Explain why serving 100 users at once can cost almost the same per step as serving 1.
5. Explain continuous batching using a restaurant, a bus or a sushi conveyor belt.
6. Explain how FlashAttention can be faster while doing *more* arithmetic (recomputation) than naive attention.
7. Explain why an outlier ruins INT8 quantization, using a ruler analogy.
8. Explain why speculative decoding can't change the model's answers.
9. Explain why a 600B-parameter MoE model can run faster per token than a 70B dense model, but still need more GPUs.
10. Explain to a product manager why putting the user's name at the start of the system prompt costs money.

## Part 3: Hands-on experiments

Small experiments that turn the theory into numbers. A single consumer or cloud GPU is enough for most of them.

### E1 · Measure prefill vs decode

Using the naive loop from [lesson 1-1](lessons/01-how-inference-works.md) with a small model, time the first token vs the rest for prompts of 100, 1,000 and 4,000 tokens. Plot TTFT against prompt length. **Expect:** TTFT grows with the prompt; per-token decode time stays nearly flat (with a KV cache).

### E2 · Find your batching curve

Run decode at batch 1, 2, 4 … 256 and record step time. Plot system tok/s and per-user tok/s. **Expect:** step time barely moves at first (memory-bound), then rises linearly once you pass the ridge or hit attention costs.

### E3 · Benchmark a real server

```
# terminal 1: start a server
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct --max-model-len 8192

# terminal 2: load-test it (see `vllm bench serve --help` for dataset options)
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts 500 --request-rate 8
```

Sweep `--request-rate` and record TTFT/TPOT p50 and p99. Find the knee. *(CLI flags change between versions, so check `--help`.)*

### E4 · Prefix caching A/B

Send requests sharing a 2,000-token system prompt, with prefix caching on and off. Compare TTFT and the hit-rate metric on `/metrics`. Then put a timestamp at the start of the prompt and watch the hit rate collapse.

### E5 · Quantize and evaluate

Serve the same model in BF16, FP8 (if your GPU supports it) and an AWQ/GPTQ INT4 checkpoint. Measure throughput at batch 1 and batch 64, and score a small eval (e.g. 100 GSM8K-style math questions). Fill in a table of speed vs accuracy.

### E6 · Profile a decode step

```
nsys profile -o trace --trace=cuda,nvtx python my_decode_loop.py
# open trace.nsys-rep in Nsight Systems: look for gaps between kernels
```

Compare eager mode, `torch.compile`, and CUDA graphs. Count kernels per step and the idle gaps.

[[play] Quiz Arcade ▶Check what stuck.](practice.md#arcade) [[prepare] Interview Prep ▶Use these numbers in interview answers.](interview.md)
